h01.

**`s3presign.Runner` (`server/runner/s3presign/runner.go:16`) — every 12 hours (plus one immediate run at startup) — wired in `server/server.go:162-171`, invoked from `Server.Start` at `server/server.go:129`.**

Details:

- **Component**: `Runner` in `server/runner/s3presign/runner.go`. Its `CheckAndPresign` pages through attachments with `StorageType = AttachmentStorageType_S3` in batches of 100 (`runner.go:52-56`), and for each one re-issues a presigned GET URL via `s3.Client.PresignGetObject` (`runner.go:106`), then writes the new URL into the attachment's `Reference` field along with an updated `LastPresignedTime` (`runner.go:112-118`).
- **Schedule**: `runnerInterval = time.Hour * 12` (`runner.go:26`), driven by a `time.Ticker` in `Run` (`runner.go:29-40`). Within each pass it skips any attachment whose presigned URL is still valid for the next 4 days — URLs are minted with a 5-day expiry, so the 12-hour cadence gives a wide refresh margin (`runner.go:82-88`).
- **Wiring**: `Server.startBackgroundRunners` constructs the runner at `server/server.go:162`, calls `RunOnce(ctx)` synchronously at `server/server.go:163` so links are fresh right after boot, then launches the ticker loop on a tracked goroutine at `server/server.go:166-171`. It's given its own cancelable context (`server/server.go:156-159`) so `Shutdown` can stop and wait for it (`server/server.go:140,143`).

The corresponding expiry is set on the S3 side in `internal/storage/s3/s3.go`, and the refreshed `Reference` is what the attachment service hands back to clients (`server/router/api/v1/attachment_service_storage.go`).

content.text:
h02.

**`webhook.Post` — `internal/webhook/webhook.go:120`; SSRF guard via `safeDialContext` / `isReservedIP` — `internal/webhook/webhook.go:59` and `internal/webhook/validate.go:44`**

**Where delivery executes.** Memo create/update/delete paths call `webhook.PostAsync` (`server/router/api/v1/memo_service_webhooks.go:43,71`), which only enqueues onto a bounded 128-slot channel (`internal/webhook/webhook.go:39,184-196`) and drops the payload with a warning if the queue is full. Four worker goroutines started in `init()` (`internal/webhook/webhook.go:42-55`) drain that queue and call `Post`, which is where the actual outbound HTTP POST happens: it marshals the payload, optionally attaches Standard Webhooks HMAC-SHA256 headers (`webhook-id`/`webhook-timestamp`/`webhook-signature`, lines 133-150), and issues `safeClient.Do(req)` at `internal/webhook/webhook.go:152`.

**What protects it.** Two layers, both keyed on `isReservedIP` (`internal/webhook/validate.go:44-54`), which tests against a set of CIDRs parsed once at startup — loopback, RFC-1918, link-local incl. `169.254.169.254` (cloud IMDS), and the IPv6 equivalents (`internal/webhook/validate.go:14-36`):

1. **Dial-time enforcement** — the shared `safeClient` uses a `Transport` whose `DialContext` is `safeDialContext` (`internal/webhook/webhook.go:32-37`). It resolves the host and refuses the connection if *any* resolved address is reserved (`internal/webhook/webhook.go:59-77`). Because the check runs at dial time rather than at configuration time, it also defeats DNS rebinding.
2. **Config-time validation** — `webhook.ValidateURL` (`internal/webhook/validate.go:62`) rejects non-`http(s)` schemes and reserved-resolving hostnames when a user saves a webhook, returning a gRPC `InvalidArgument` (`server/router/api/v1/user_service_webhooks.go:74,161,182`).

One caveat worth noting: the package-level `AllowPrivateIPs` flag (`internal/webhook/validate.go:41`) short-circuits both layers when true, for self-hosted setups targeting LAN services. I found no code in the repo that ever sets it, so it is effectively always `false` (protection on) unless something outside this tree assigns it.

**`internal/idp` (abstraction); `internal/idp/oauth2` (implementation)**

**No — the only production construction site is the factory.** One in-package test builds a zero-value `&DB{}`, which is worth naming but isn't a driver instantiation.

1. **The package is imported exactly once in the whole tree.** `grep -rn "usememos/memos/store/db/mysql" --include=*.go` returns a single hit: `store/db/db.go:8`. No other Go file — production or test — imports `store/db/mysql`, so `mysql.NewDB` is unreachable from anywhere else. The sole call is `store/db/db.go:22`, inside `NewDBDriver`'s `case "mysql":` switch.

2. **`NewDB` is the only exported constructor**, defined at `store/db/mysql/mysql.go:20`. It returns the interface type `store.Driver`, not `*DB`, and it's the only place `DB`'s unexported fields (`db`, `profile`, `config` — `store/db/mysql/mysql.go:14-18`) are populated.

4. **The one direct struct literal is in-package and inert.** `store/db/mysql/auth_config_test.go:12` does `db := &DB{}` — but that file is `package mysql`, so it isn't "outside the factory" in the import sense, and the zero-value struct has a nil `*sql.DB`. h05.

**Explicit Go code — two separate `DELETE FROM reaction` statements inside the user-deletion transaction, in all three drivers. There is no database-level rule that would do it.**

What I checked:

**1. The delete path.** `Store.DeleteUser` (`store/user.go:171-181`) delegates straight to `s.driver.DeleteUser`. Each driver runs the whole teardown in one transaction and calls `deleteUserTargetsTx`, which removes reactions in two passes (`store/db/mysql/user_delete.go:88-99`, and the identical sequence at `store/db/sqlite/user_delete.go:96,102` and `store/db/postgres/user_delete.go:96,102`):

- `deleteReactionsByContentIDsTx` — reactions *on* the user's memos, i.e. other people's reactions to their content. Content IDs are built as `"memos/"+memo.UID` (`store/db/mysql/user_delete.go:508-514`) from the full memo tree (roots plus `COMMENT`-related descendants, `listDeleteUserMemoTreeIterative`), then deleted with `DELETE FROM reaction WHERE content_id IN (...)` in batches of 500 (`store/db/mysql/user_delete.go:397-405`).
- `deleteReactionsByCreatorTx` — reactions *by* the user on anyone's content: `DELETE FROM reaction WHERE creator_id = ?` (`store/db/mysql/user_delete.go:417-420`).

Both run before the memo rows and the `user` row are deleted, within the same `tx`.

**2. Ruled out a database-level rule.** The `reaction` table carries no foreign key at all — `creator_id INTEGER NOT NULL` and `content_id TEXT NOT NULL` are plain columns with only a `UNIQUE(creator_id, content_id, reaction_type)` constraint. Same in all three dialects: `store/migration/sqlite/LATEST.sql:91-99`, `store/migration/postgres/LATEST.sql:90-98`, `store/migration/mysql/LATEST.sql` (reaction block), and the original `0.20/00__reaction.sql` files. Grepping `FOREIGN KEY|REFERENCES|CASCADE` across all `LATEST.sql` files yields exactly one cascade in each dialect, and it's on `memo_share.memo_id → memo(id)` (`store/migration/sqlite/LATEST.sql:109`), not on `reaction`. Additionally, `content_id` is a string like `memos/<uid>` rather than a numeric memo id, so an FK cascade wouldn't be expressible there anyway.

**3. Even if a constraint existed, SQLite wouldn't enforce it** — the connection opens with `_pragma=foreign_keys(0)` (`store/db/sqlite/sqlite.go:53`), which is consistent with the codebase handling referential cleanup in Go rather than relying on the engine.

| Handler | Path to dispatch |
|---|---|
| `CreateMemo` (`memo_service.go:70`) | `DispatchMemoCreatedWebhook` at `memo_service.go:157` |
| `UpdateMemo` (`memo_service.go:401`) | `dispatchMemoUpdatedSideEffects` at `memo_service.go:513` → `DispatchMemoUpdatedWebhook` (`memo_update_helpers.go:67`) |
| `DeleteMemo` (`memo_service.go:518`) | `DispatchMemoDeletedWebhook` at `memo_service.go:562` |
| `CreateMemoComment` (`memo_service_comments.go:20`) | `DispatchMemoCommentCreatedWebhook` at `memo_service_comments.go:119` — notably fires at the *related memo owner's* webhooks, not the commenter's |
| `SetMemoRelations` (`memo_relation_service.go:16`) | `dispatchMemoUpdatedSideEffects` at `memo_relation_service.go:48` |
| `SetMemoAttachments` (`memo_attachment_service.go:16`) | `dispatchMemoUpdatedSideEffects` at `memo_attachment_service.go:48` |

Notes on the path:

- **Wiring**: the service is constructed and its routes registered at `server/server.go:81-82`.
- **Access control** happens before any lookup: if `s.Profile.AllowAnonymous()` is false, `getCurrentUser` must resolve a session/access token/PAT or the handler returns 401 (`fileserver.go:170-179`). On a public instance, anyone may fetch any user's avatar.

**`(*renderer).addArg` — `internal/filter/render.go:842` — ~28 call sites (14 distinct calling methods)**

How I measured: I extracted all 272 non-test `func` declarations under `internal/` (151 package-level functions, 121 methods) and counted matching call sites across every non-test `.go` file in the repo, excluding declaration lines. Ranked results:

| Symbol | Path | Raw hits | Real? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `New` | three packages | 307 | ✗ — `New(` collides with unrelated constructors everywhere |
| `(*Schedule).Next` | `internal/scheduler/parser.go:92` | 55 | ✗ — almost all are `sql.Rows.Next()` in `store/db/*`; only **1** real caller, `internal/scheduler/scheduler.go:142` |
| **`(*renderer).addArg`** | `internal/filter/render.go:842` | **28** | ✓ — all 28 are `r.addArg(` in `internal/filter/render.go` |
| `Schema.Field` | `internal/filter/schema.go:67` | 19 | ✓ — runner-up; 10 in `internal/filter/parser.go`, 9 in `internal/filter/render.go` |
| `s3.NewClient` / `email.NewClient` | `internal/storage/s3/s3.go:25` | 18 combined | ✗ — the two names collide; `s3.NewClient` alone is ~5 |
| `jsonArrayExpr` | `internal/filter/render.go:944` | 16 | ✓ |

`addArg` is the SQL-argument accumulator for the filter-to-SQL renderer: it bumps `placeholderCounter`, appends the value to `r.args`, and returns the dialect-correct placeholder (`$N` for Postgres, `?` otherwise). Essentially every render path that emits a bound value calls it, which is why the fan-in is concentrated: all 28 sites are inside `render.go`, spread across 14 distinct `(*renderer)` methods (comparison, IN, text-match, tag-comprehension, and JSON rendering paths).

Two caveats on the number. It's a textual call-site count, not a static-analysis call graph — I counted occurrences of `.addArg(`, which is unambiguous here since `renderer` is package-private to `internal/filter` and no other type in the tree declares that method. And if you define fan-in as *distinct callers* rather than call sites, the figure is 14, which still leads (`Schema.Field`'s 19 sites also spread across roughly that many functions, so the two are close on that metric).

h12.

**`(*sqlite.DB).CreateMemo` — `store/db/sqlite/memo.go:16`; determined by resolving the runtime driver-selection chain from the CLI default through the factory, since the interface has three implementations**

The INSERT itself is built at `store/db/sqlite/memo.go:41`:
```
INSERT INTO `memo` (`uid`, `creator_id`, `content`, `visibility`, `payload`[, `created_ts`][, `updated_ts`])
VALUES (...) RETURNING `id`, `created_ts`, `updated_ts`, `row_status`
```
executed via `d.db.QueryRowContext` at `store/db/sqlite/memo.go:42`.

**How I determined it was the SQLite one rather than the Postgres or MySQL sibling** — the call path is interface-dispatched, so the concrete target isn't visible from the call site. I resolved it by following the value that gets bound at startup:

1. **Call site is abstract.** The handler `CreateMemo` calls `s.Store.CreateMemo` (`server/router/api/v1/memo_service.go:115`), which validates the UID and delegates to `s.driver.CreateMemo` (`store/memo.go:109-114`). `s.driver` is typed `store.Driver` (`store/driver.go`) — an interface with three implementations: `store/db/sqlite/memo.go:16`, `store/db/postgres/memo.go`, `store/db/mysql/memo.go`.

2. **The interface value is assigned once, in the factory.** `NewDBDriver` switches on `profile.Driver` and returns `sqlite.NewDB` / `mysql.NewDB` / `postgres.NewDB` (`store/db/db.go:14-28`). That driver is handed to `store.New(dbDriver, instanceProfile)` at `cmd/memos/main.go:63` and never reassigned — grepping for imports of `store/db/mysql` and `store/db/postgres` confirms `store/db/db.go` is their only importer, so no other construction site exists.

3. **The default value of `profile.Driver` is `"sqlite"`.** Set twice in the CLI: `viper.SetDefault("driver", "sqlite")` (`cmd/memos/main.go:122`) and the flag default `rootCmd.PersistentFlags().String("driver", "sqlite", ...)` (`cmd/memos/main.go:130`), bound together at `cmd/memos/main.go:151`. The profile is populated from `viper.GetString("driver")` at `cmd/memos/main.go:43`. `Profile.Validate` (`internal/profile/profile.go:70`) defaults the data dir but doesn't alter `Driver`, so with no flags/env the switch takes `case "sqlite"`.

So on a default install the chain is: `CreateMemo` handler → `Store.CreateMemo` → `Driver.CreateMemo` (interface) → `(*sqlite.DB).CreateMemo`. The Postgres and MySQL `CreateMemo` methods are compiled in but unreachable unless `--driver` (or the corresponding env/config value) says otherwise.

**Premise correction: there is no Redis in this repository.** Grepping `redis` case-insensitively across all Go sources, `go.mod`, `go.sum`, and YAML/JSON config returns zero hits. The cache layer is entirely in-process — there is no external cache server, no connection string, and nothing to configure.

**Actual mechanism.** The cache is a hand-rolled in-memory implementation in `store/cache/cache.go`: a `sync.Map` of `item{value, expiration, size}` guarded by an atomic item counter, satisfying the local `cache.Interface` (`store/cache/cache.go:11-32`).

Three separate `*cache.Cache` instances hang off `Store` (`store/store.go:27-29`): `instanceSettingCache`, `userCache`, and `userSettingCache`. All three are built in `store.New` from one hardcoded `cache.Config` (`store/store.go:40-53`):

- `DefaultTTL: 10 * time.Minute`
- `CleanupInterval: 5 * time.Minute`
- `MaxItems: 1000`
- `OnEviction: nil`

**TTL for user entries: 10 minutes.** Every write goes through `Set` (`store/user.go:98,122,132,143,167`), and `Cache.Set` delegates to `SetWithTTL(ctx, key, value, c.config.DefaultTTL)` (`store/cache/cache.go:94`) — nothing in the user path calls `SetWithTTL` with a custom duration, so the 10-minute default is what applies. Keys are `userCacheKey(user.ID)`. The same 10 minutes applies to instance settings and user settings, since they share the config literal.

Two details that matter more than the TTL in practice: the cache is only consulted on ID-keyed lookups — `Store.GetUser` skips it entirely when finding by username or other fields (`store/user.go:149-156`) — and entries are invalidated eagerly on mutation and delete rather than being left to expire (`Store.DeleteUser` → `s.deleteUserCache`, `store/user.go:179`). Cleanup goroutines are stopped via `Store.Close` → `userCache.Close()` (`store/store.go:75`). Since the cache lives in the process, it is per-instance and not shared across replicas.

`DefaultConfig()` in `store/cache/cache.go:56-63` declares the identical values, but `store.New` builds its own literal rather than calling it.

- **Content-length limits** on memos, read from instance settings (`server/router/api/v1/memo_service.go:595`).

These bound the size and concurrency of individual operations; none limits how many requests a user may issue over time. **Premise correction: there is no nightly database-cleanup job, and the cron scheduler has no registered jobs at all — so there is no time to report.**

Two separate corrections:

1. **The cron scheduler is never used in production.** `internal/scheduler` is a complete, working package — cron-expression parsing (`internal/scheduler/parser.go:30`), `Register`/`Start`/`Stop` (`internal/scheduler/scheduler.go:70,91,169`), timezone and middleware options (`Recovery`, `Logging`, `Timeout` in `internal/scheduler/middleware.go`) — but nothing imports it. The server never constructs a `Scheduler`, so no cron expression is ever registered or evaluated at runtime.

2. **There is no database-cleanup job to schedule.** No vacuum, purge, prune, or retention routine exists. The only background work the server actually starts is the S3 presign refresher — `startBackgroundRunners` creates and runs `s3presign.Runner` (`server/server.go:162-171`), which is driven by a plain `time.Ticker` at a 12-hour interval (`server/runner/s3persign/runner.go` → `server/runner/s3presign/runner.go:26,29-40`), not by the cron scheduler and not at a wall-clock time.

Deletion cleanup in this codebase is **event-driven, not scheduled**: it happens inline in the request that triggers it — the transactional cascade in `DeleteUser` (`store/db/sqlite/user_delete.go`, and the Postgres/MySQL peers), memo deletion handling relations and attachments (`server/router/api/v1/memo_service.go:579`), and S3 object cleanup during attachment deletion (`store/attachment.go:171`).

The closest thing to a recurring "cleanup" is the in-memory cache's expiry sweep — `cleanupLoop` on a 5-minute `CleanupInterval` (`store/cache/cache.go:60,83`) — but that evicts cache entries, touches no database, and again uses a ticker rather than cron.

**Premise correction: there is no GraphQL in this repository.** A case-insensitive grep for `graphql|gqlgen|apollo|.graphql` across Go sources, `go.mod`, TypeScript/TSX, and JSON config returns zero hits — no schema file, no resolver layer, no client library on either the server or the web side.

**Actual API surface: Protocol Buffers / gRPC, exposed over three transports.**

The schema of record is the set of `.proto` service definitions in `proto/api/v1/` — `memo_service.proto`, `user_service.proto`, `auth_service.proto`, `attachment_service.proto`, `instance_service.proto`, `idp_service.proto`, `shortcut_service.proto`, `ai_service.proto`, plus `common.proto`. A parallel `proto/store/` tree defines persisted payload messages (e.g. the `MemoPayload` used for derived metadata). API design follows Google's AIPs, per `proto/api/v1/README.md`.

Code generation is driven by buf (`proto/buf.gen.yaml`, `buf.yaml`, `buf.lock`) with five server-side plugins plus one for the frontend, all emitting into `proto/gen/` (and `web/src/types/proto` for TypeScript):

- `protocolbuffers/go` — message types
- `grpc/go` — gRPC service stubs
- `connectrpc/go` — Connect handlers (`proto/gen/api/v1/apiv1connect/`)
- `grpc-ecosystem/gateway` — REST/JSON transcoding (`*.pb.gw.go`)
- `community/google-gnostic-openapi` — an OpenAPI document, embedded via `proto/openapi_embed.go`
- `bufbuild/es` — TypeScript types for the web client

At runtime, `APIV1Service.RegisterGateway` (`server/router/api/v1/v1.go:65`) mounts two of these onto Echo: the **gRPC-Gateway** mux for REST-style JSON calls (`v1.go:95`), and **Connect** handlers for browser clients — replacing grpc-web — served on the `/memos.api.v1.*` path group with a request-size cap (`v1.go:131-144`). Both share one authorizer so auth policy has a single source of truth (`v1.go:67`).

So the equivalent of "where the schema is defined" is `proto/api/v1/*.proto`; the closest analogue to a queryable public schema document is the generated OpenAPI spec rather than a GraphQL SDL.
